prompt.context: Our client is a regional electricity monopoly. Due to regulation, its market will be opened to competition next year on January 1. There are no actual competitors at this time; however, the client would like ideas on actions to take in the short-term in order to better prepare for potential competitors. They have no control over pricing and cost-cutting during this time period.
prompt.question: What actions should Central Power take in the short-term to prepare for competition entering its market?

clarifying_info.q: Do we know of any potential competitors?
clarifying_info.a: None at this time. Central Power is facing the threat of market entry.

clarifying_info.q: Do you have any information on pricing?
clarifying_info.a: Not really; pricing is controlled by a government, so it is beyond our control and will be the same for any competition.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other markets Central Power can enter?
clarifying_info.a: None at this time. Our engagement is focused on their home market.
Central Power has three divisions: 1. Sales and General Administration, 2. Generation and Transmission, 3. Maintenance and Repair.

clarifying_info.q: How many employees are in sales?
Does sales or customer service treat certain customer segments differently?
If there is a power outage, does Maintenance and Repair fix industrial clients first?
clarifying_info.a: No, they dispatch in the order of the call they receive.

clarifying_info.q: Has Central Power ever advertised or had a marketing campaign?
Is Central Power undertaking any capital investment?

exhibits.title: Central Power Revenue by Customer Segment
exhibits.shows: A chart displaying Central Power's revenue broken down by customer segment (Industrial, Commercial, Residential), including historical revenue data and number of customers per segment.
exhibits.data: Industrial: 150 customers, $150MM revenue; Commercial: 10,000 customers, $60MM revenue; Residential: 100,000 customers, $48MM revenue; Total revenue approximately $258MM.

framework: Barriers to Entry: assess what internal barriers can be raised (e.g., switching costs, commercial attractiveness) since external/regulatory barriers and pricing are not options
Anticipation of Competitive Attack: identify which customer segments a rational competitor would target first upon market entry
Market Information: analyze revenue and customer segmentation to understand relative value of each segment
Customer Retention Initiatives: generate ideas across the value chain (Sales & Admin, Generation & Transmission, Maintenance & Repair) to improve retention, especially for high-value segments
Stakeholder Reactions: consider how employees, unions, and local government leaders will react to proposed changes

questions.prompt: What is your reaction to the revenue exhibit? Calculate the share of total revenue per segment and the revenue per customer for each segment.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates immediately notice the dramatic difference in per-customer value across segments. Industrial customers are a tiny group (150) generating 58% of revenue ($1M each), while 100,000 residential customers generate only 19% of revenue ($480 each). Losing a single industrial customer equates to losing ~2,083 residential customers. Candidates should then conclude that any action must be biased toward retaining industrial and commercial customers.

math.setup: Total revenue = $150MM + $60MM + $48MM = $258MM. Revenue per customer = segment revenue / number of customers. Share = segment revenue / $258MM.
steps: Residential customer equivalents of one industrial customer: $1,000,000 / $480 = ~2,083
math.answer: Industrial customers are worth ~$1M each (58% of total revenue from only 150 customers); commercial ~$6,000 each; residential ~$480 each. One industrial customer is worth roughly 2,083 residential customers.

questions.prompt: Based on the data, if you were a competitor entering this market, which segment would you target and why?
questions.guidance: Candidates should identify industrial customers as the prime target for a new entrant: highest revenue per customer, fewest customers to win over, and largest revenue impact per defection. This insight should then drive Central Power's defensive strategy — protect industrial customers first.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific actions can Central Power take across its three divisions — Sales & General Administration, Generation & Transmission, and Maintenance & Repair — to improve customer retention, particularly for industrial and commercial clients?

categories.name: Sales and General Administration
ideas: Sign long-term customer contracts to increase switching costs
Increase credit terms / extend days allowable for accounts receivable
Increase the size of the sales force
Allocate sales staff to specific customer segments (B2B vs. residential) since the value proposition differs
Assign dedicated personal account managers to high-value industrial accounts
Reduce or simplify the billing process
Create a website or online portal for customers to manage accounts

categories.name: Generation and Transmission
ideas: Build substations or add redundancy to improve reliability and power quality for industrial clients
Work with industrial clients to improve their energy efficiency (value-added advisory service)

categories.name: Maintenance and Repair
ideas: Prioritize outage repairs by customer value (industrial first) rather than first-come, first-served
Pre-position repair equipment near clusters of industrial clients to reduce repair time
Proactively visit industrial clients to inspect their infrastructure or provide engineering advice

recommendation: By investigating the operations of your company, we have developed several ideas for strengthening customer retention in the face of competition.

No matter which actions are undertaken, there should be a bias towards industrial customers, who are more valuable both as a group (58% of revenue) and on a per-customer basis ($1M vs. $480 for residential).
If any of these actions seem attractive to management, we can undertake more detailed analysis to support prioritization.
risks: Employee and union resistance to changes in work practices (e.g., new dispatch prioritization, dedicated account teams)
Local government or regulatory pushback on differentiated service levels
Short implementation timeline (less than one year before deregulation)
next_steps: Analyze costs, potential ROI, and stakeholder effects for each customer retention initiative
Prioritize initiatives by impact on industrial customer retention vs. implementation complexity
Develop a stakeholder communication plan for employees, unions, and government leaders
